issues.display_title: Issue #129: Scrollbar on Preview Page is Too Thin and Hard to Grab
issues.main_description_html:
Demo by developer

Image Issue

Problem

The scrollbar on the Preview page is too thin to see and almost impossible to grab. The
track is 4px wide (2px tall for horizontal), so catching the thumb needs pixel-perfect
mouse precision and the scroll position is hard to read at a glance.

Steps to reproduce

  1. Open Preview on a folder with more images than fit on screen
  2. Look at the scrollbar on the right of the browse grid
  3. Try to click and drag the thumb

The bar is barely visible and the cursor slips off the thumb.

Expected

The scrollbar is thick enough to see and to click/hold/drag without precise aiming,
closer to a standard application scrollbar, and stays consistent in light and dark mode.

Note

The scrollbar is styled globally, not per page — src/renderer/index.css sets
::-webkit-scrollbar for the whole app, so this affects every scrollable area, not just
Preview.

Fix in progress on feat/renderer-refactor-g0:

  • src/renderer/index.css — ::-webkit-scrollbar width 4px -> 8px, height 2px -> 6px

Thumb/track colours and radius are unchanged; the hidden-scrollbar cases
(scrollbar-width: none utility, .rename-input) stay hidden as before.

issues.display_title: Issue #130: Windows uninstaller uses the default NSIS icon, not the app logo
issues.main_description_html:
Demo by developer

Image Issue

Problem

The Windows uninstaller shows the generic NSIS icon instead of the GoThru Photo Studio
logo. The installer itself is branded correctly, so the mismatch only shows up when the
user uninstalls.

Steps to reproduce

  1. Install the app on Windows with the NSIS installer
  2. Open the install folder (%LOCALAPPDATA%\GoThru Photo Studio or the chosen $INSTDIR)
  3. Look at uninstall.exe, or launch it and look at the window/taskbar icon

The icon is the default NSIS uninstall icon (grey box with a red X), not the app logo.

Expected

The uninstaller uses the app icon (icons/icon.ico), same as the installer.

Note

Root cause: Tauri's NSIS template does !define MUI_UNICON "${UNINSTALLERICON}", and
UNINSTALLERICON is only defined when the config sets nsis.uninstallerIcon.
tauri.windows.conf.json only set installerIcon, so the uninstaller fell back to the
NSIS default.

The Apps & Features entry is not affected — the template already writes
DisplayIcon = "$INSTDIR\GoThru Photo Studio.exe", which resolves to the app icon.

Fix on feat/renderer-refactor-g0:

  • src-tauri/tauri.windows.conf.json — add "uninstallerIcon": "icons/icon.ico" to
    bundle.windows.nsis

Verification

Not verifiable from macOS — needs a pnpm tauri build on Windows, then check the icon on
uninstall.exe in the install folder.

issues.display_title: Issue #140: AI Nadir Output Routing Fails When Processing Multiple Folders
issues.main_description_html:
Demo by developer

Video.Project.13.mp4

Image Issue

Description

A regression has been identified in the new version of GoThru Photo Studio regarding batch processing across multiple directories.

When a user attempts to apply the AI Nadir tool to images originating from multiple different folders (e.g., 10 different folders), the output routing logic fails. Instead of creating a designated output sub-folder under each respective parent folder and saving the patched images there, the application creates only one single output folder and dumps all patched images from all 10 folders into it. This creates a disorganized mess for the user and breaks the expected workflow.

Note: This feature worked correctly in the previous version of the application.

Steps to Reproduce

  1. Open GoThru Photo Studio.
  2. Select or queue images that are located across multiple separate folders (e.g., Folder A, Folder B, Folder C).
  3. Apply the AI Nadir patching tool to the entire selection.
  4. Observe the output directory generation once processing is complete.
  5. Actual Result: All images are dumped into a single sub-folder, mixing the contents of Folder A, B, and C.
  6. Expected Result: A new sub-folder should be created inside Folder A for Folder A's images, another inside Folder B for Folder B's images, etc.

Acceptance Criteria

  1. Applying the AI Nadir tool to images spanning multiple folders correctly generates a separate output sub-folder within each respective parent folder.
  2. Patched images are saved strictly within their correct parent folder's hierarchy.
  3. No cross-contamination of images occurs between different folders.

Source Note

Reported by albug: applying AI Nadir to images from 10 folders should create one output sub-folder under each source folder; the new version currently creates a single output folder and mixes all patched images there.

issues.display_title: Issue #150: Auto Level freezes the whole device on lower-spec machines
issues.main_description_html:
What happened

A client reported that their entire device freezes — not just our app — while running
Auto Level. Mouse and other programs become unresponsive too.

Reproduced internally: CPU sits at 100% during generating, but the system stays usable. So
the freeze only shows up on machines with lower specs.

Why it happens

Two separate issues that make each other worse.

1. Auto Level uses too much memory at once.

While processing, it holds two full copies of the panorama in RAM at the same time — the
original and the corrected version. The original is kept around longer than it needs to be,
well past the point where it's still used.

For a high-resolution panorama that's roughly 800 MB – 1.2 GB of RAM for a single photo.
On a machine with 8 GB, once other apps are running, the system runs out of RAM and starts
swapping to disk. That's what freezes the whole device. The 100% CPU reading is misleading —
at that point it's disk thrashing, not actual work.

2. Auto Level uses every CPU core, leaving none for the UI.

There's no limit on how many cores the processing takes. On a machine with many cores, the
UI still gets enough time to stay responsive. On a 4-core machine, nothing is left over and
the app stops responding.

The same pattern exists in the equirectangular rotate feature, so it likely has the same
problem.

Proposed fix

  1. Release the original image from memory as soon as it's no longer needed, before the
    output is encoded. Cuts peak memory roughly in half. Biggest win for the least work.
  2. Cap how many CPU cores the processing can use, always leaving one free for the UI.
    Processing gets slightly slower, but the app stays responsive — progress stays visible and
    Cancel still works. This fixes the rotate feature at the same time.
  3. Minor: a stale comment in the Auto Level code still claims it runs an external binary. It
    hasn't since the native migration — worth correcting so it doesn't mislead later.

Output quality and accuracy are unaffected. This is purely about how the work is scheduled
and how memory is held.

Not doing for now: encoding straight to disk instead of buffering in memory, and processing
the image in bands instead of allocating the full output up front. Both are bigger reworks —
revisit only if (1) and (2) turn out to be insufficient.

Still to confirm

The memory analysis is confirmed from the code. What isn't confirmed is that it's the cause
of this client's freeze specifically. Requested from them:

  • RAM and CPU core count
  • Resolution of the panorama being processed
  • Whether the Memory column in Task Manager maxes out during the freeze

After the fix: measure peak memory before/after on a large panorama, and verify the UI stays
responsive throughout.

Where to look

src-tauri/src/pano_level/ (the processing pipeline) and
src-tauri/src/commands/auto_level.rs (the queue). Detailed allocation trace with line
numbers available on request.

📄 Client-facing report sent to the client — click to expand

Non-technical version written for the client. Kept here verbatim as a record of what was
communicated, and of what we committed to.

Report: Device Slowdown / Freeze When Using Auto Level

Status: Cause identified — fix in preparation
Date: 31 July 2026

Summary

We've investigated your report about your device freezing while running the Auto Level
feature, and we've found the cause.

This is not damage to the application or to your photo files. The process runs correctly
and the results remain accurate — the issue is with how much of your computer's resources
are being used while it runs. On devices with more limited specifications, that usage
exceeds what's available, which causes the entire system to slow down.

We've already planned the fix, and it requires nothing on your end.

What Is Actually Happening

Auto Level works by loading the entire panorama into memory (RAM), analysing its tilt, and
then repositioning every single point in the image to the correct place.

Because 360° panorama photos are very large, this process requires:

1. A large amount of memory (RAM)

While running, the application needs to hold two copies of the photo in memory at the
same time: the original and the corrected version. For a high-resolution panorama, this can
consume roughly 800 MB to 1.2 GB of RAM for a single photo.

When the available RAM runs out, the operating system starts moving data to the hard disk as
backup memory. That process is far slower — and it's what makes the entire device, not
just our application, feel frozen.

2. Every processor (CPU) core

To keep processing fast, Auto Level currently uses all available processor cores. On a
computer with many cores this is fine — there's still spare capacity left to run the
application's interface. But on a computer with fewer cores, there's no spare capacity at
all, so the interface stops responding while the process runs.

Why It Doesn't Happen on Every Device

We tested this on our internal devices and the process ran normally — CPU usage did reach
100%, but the system stayed responsive.

The difference comes down to device specifications:

Higher-spec device Lower-spec device
RAM Enough to hold two copies of the photo Not enough → system falls back to the hard disk → drastic slowdown
CPU cores Spare capacity left for the interface Fully consumed → application stops responding
Result Feels heavy but keeps running Feels like a complete freeze

So the symptoms you're experiencing are an expected outcome — and something we can fully
address from the application side.

The Planned Fix

We've prepared two main improvements:

Fix 1 — Significantly reduce memory usage

We'll change the process so that the original copy of the photo is released from memory
earlier, as soon as it's no longer needed. The effect: peak RAM usage drops by roughly
half.

This is the change that matters most for devices with limited RAM.

Fix 2 — Reserve processor capacity for the interface

We'll limit how many processor cores are used, so there's always capacity left to run the
application's interface. Processing may take slightly longer, but the application will
stay responsive throughout — you'll still be able to see progress, cancel the process, or
switch between menus.

This improvement will also apply to other features with a similar processing pattern.

What won't change: the quality and accuracy of Auto Level's results stay exactly the
same. These changes only affect how the application manages resource usage, not how it
corrects your photos.

What You Can Do In The Meantime

While waiting for the update, these steps should help:

  1. Close other applications before running Auto Level — especially your browser, as
    browsers typically consume the most RAM.
  2. Process in smaller batches — add a few photos per queue rather than dozens at once.
  3. Let the process run undisturbed — avoid force-closing the application when it appears
    frozen. In many cases the process is still running and will finish on its own.
  4. Reduce photo resolution where possible — the larger the panorama, the more memory it
    requires.

Information We Need From You

To make sure our fix actually resolves the problem on your device — rather than solving a
different one — we'd appreciate the following information:

  1. Device specifications: RAM capacity and processor type
    (Windows: right-click Start → System)
  2. Resolution of the panorama photo being processed when the freeze occurred
    (for example: 16000 × 8000 pixels)
  3. Number of photos in the queue when the problem appeared
  4. Conditions during the freeze: did only our application stop responding, or did the
    entire device freeze as well (mouse cursor stuttering too)?
  5. If possible: open Task Manager while the process is running, and note whether the
    figure in the Memory column climbs close to its maximum.

Items 1, 2, and 5 are the most helpful to us.

Next Steps

  1. We receive your device information
  2. We complete and test both fixes described above
  3. We re-test under conditions resembling your device
  4. The fix is released through an application update

We'll notify you as soon as the update is ready. If you have any questions, or notice any
other symptoms, please let us know.

Thank you for the report — reports like this genuinely help us improve the application for
all our users.

issues.display_title: Issue #124: Nadir Builder: dropping a logo on the drop zone does nothing
issues.main_description_html:
Demo by developer

2026-07-31.17-19-09.mp4

Problem

Dropping a logo image from Finder/Explorer onto the Nadir Builder drop zone does nothing.
The zone never reacts and the logo is not queued.

Steps to reproduce

  1. Open Edit → Nadir Builder
  2. Drag a .png / .jpg logo from Finder over the "drag & drop" zone
  3. Release

Nothing happens — no toast, no logo loaded.

Expected

Dropping a valid image queues it as the nadir logo (same as picking it via the file
dialog), with the existing validation toasts for multiple files / wrong extension.

Note

Same root cause as #120/#122: the Tauri webview swallows OS file drops before DOM
onDrop handlers fire, so LogoDropZone's DOM handlers are dead in the app.

Fix in progress on feat/renderer-refactor-g0: LogoDropZone subscribes to
ipc.onOsFileDrop, hit-tests the drop position against its own rect and hands the real
paths to a new handleDropLogoPaths in useNadirBuilder (same validation as the DOM
path, no resolveDroppedFilePath needed).

Other Edit features with the same dead DOM drop zones (candidates for the same fix):
LogoPatching, MinifyJpg, Enfuse, ImageStraightener, ImageResize, ImageToVideo.

issues.display_title: Issue #122: Drag and drop from Browse to the map does not set the marker
issues.main_description_html:
Demo by developer

2026-07-31.17-15-05.mp4

Problem

Dragging an image from the Browse list onto the map does not set the marker. The drop is
silently ignored, so the image never gets the drop position assigned as its GPS location
(pre-merge test plan scenario M5). Dropping files from Finder into the app works; only
drags that start inside the app are affected.

Steps to reproduce

  1. Open Preview on a folder of images
  2. Show the map (corner map or split screen)
  3. Drag an image from the Browse list and drop it on a map location

The marker does not move and the image's GPS data is unchanged.

Expected

Dropping an image on the map assigns the drop position to that image and moves the
marker there, same as the Electron app.

Note

Root cause: the Browse drag is a native OS drag (ipc.startDrag -> Rust drag crate),
and wry only reports drops of external drag sessions (e.g. from Finder) — drags
started by the app's own process are never delivered to onDragDropEvent, so no
renderer listener can ever see them.

Fix in progress on feat/renderer-refactor-g0:

  • commands/desktop.rs — ondragstart's drag-end callback now emits app:drag-drop
    (paths + cursor position relative to the window) so in-app targets hear about the drop
  • src/lib/ipc.ts — bridges both wry's onDragDropEvent and app:drag-drop into one
    ipc.onOsFileDrop channel (drop position normalised from physical to client pixels)
  • Map/hooks/useMapDragDrop.ts — hit-tests the drop against the map container,
    unprojects to lng/lat and calls updateGPSData
  • Drag ghost reworked: small thumbnail of the dragged image with a native-style green
    "+" badge (app-icon ghost confused the drop affordance)

issues.display_title: Issue #120: Drag and drop files into the app does not work
issues.main_description_html:
Demo by developer

2026-07-31.17-03-05.mp4

Problem

Dragging files from Finder/Explorer onto the app to upload does nothing. The drop is
ignored — no files are added, no error shown.

Steps to reproduce

  1. Open the app on the Upload screen
  2. Drag one or more image files from Finder (or Explorer) over the app window
  3. Release over the drop area

Nothing happens; the files are not picked up.

Expected

Dropping files onto the app adds them to the upload list, same as the Electron app.

Note

Likely cause: Tauri v2 has dragDropEnabled: true by default (nothing set in
src-tauri/tauri.conf.json), which makes the webview intercept OS file drops — HTML5
onDrop handlers in the renderer never fire. Fix is either listening via
getCurrentWebview().onDragDropEvent(...) or setting dragDropEnabled: false on the
window so the HTML5 events reach the renderer again.

Problem

S1 (the Upload refactor, PR #134) merged into development on static gates only — pnpm typecheck,
pnpm lint, pnpm test. No part of it has been driven by hand. Native dialogs, Google OAuth and
real upload targets cannot be automated, so nothing has verified that the three upload modals still
work.

The two tasks that need hands on them:

  • Task 4 (d1fff16) replaced three near-copies of the provider modal with one shared shell plus
    one login form. GoThru, Panorra and Street View now render through the same component.
  • Task 5 (0565ff5) replaced eight hand-rolled sendMessage + onRendererMessage pairs with
    ipc.request, changing the async contract behind every login, account switch, account removal and
    account list load.

Task 3 (5544f71) also moved processingFiles from filesSlice into uploadSlice, so the upload
progress panel and Eq2Photo capture read a different slice than before.

What to do

Run docs/refactor/s1-upload-test-plan.md top to bottom on a real build (pnpm tauri dev or a
release build — note which).

Section 4.1 has to run three times, once per target (GoThru / Panorra / Street View), each with a
real upload. One shell serves all three now, so a pass on one proves nothing about the others.

Requirements for the run:

  • A GoThru account, a Panorra account, a Google account with Street View
  • Two accounts on at least one target — switch account, set-default and remove cannot be tested
    with one
  • 2–3 real panoramas to upload
  • Devtools open the whole run; Redux serializable/immutable warnings are findings

Expected

Every scenario in the plan passes, or fails into its own issue. Sign-off section filled in at the
bottom of the plan.

Note

Section 3 of the plan lists behaviour that did change and is not a regression — the paths that
used to hang forever now time out after 15s (ipc.request default). Section 5 lists the five
provider differences S1 deliberately kept rather than normalised away; those are not findings
either.

Known open Upload issues #106 and #120 are out of scope for this run — S1 changed structure only.

This is the gate before the next development → master merge.

Problem

S4 (the Preference refactor, PR #141, 56ca4ad) merged into development on static gates only —
pnpm typecheck, pnpm lint, pnpm test. The test plan was written and never run.

The phase split the two worst files in the app by lines-per-file: ApiKey (516) and Preference
(483), both settings forms doing validation, IPC and layout in one place. Splitting a form that
persists API keys and app settings is exactly the change that compiles clean and still writes the
wrong value.

What to do

Run docs/refactor/s4-preference-test-plan.md top to bottom on a real build (pnpm tauri dev or a
release build — note which).

Requirements for the run:

  • Real API keys for every provider the settings page accepts — a saved-but-wrong key is the failure
    mode, and it is invisible until a feature that uses it runs
  • Restart the app after saving, to prove persistence survives the process, not just the store
  • Devtools open the whole run; Redux serializable/immutable warnings are findings

Expected

Every scenario in the plan passes, or fails into its own issue. Sign-off section filled in at the
bottom of the plan.

Note

Phase context and status: docs/refactor/s-phases.md. This is one of the gates before the next
development → master merge.

Record

S5 (the Preview refactor, PR #142, 4599a7c) merged into development, and it is the only S
phase so far whose manual pass was executed before merge.

docs/refactor/s5-preview-test-plan.md was run and passed. Filed for the record so the board shows
which phases carry QA debt and which do not.

Scope covered

The largest non-Edit feature — 40 files / 6.2k lines, every viewer path. Includes the Preview-specific
modals taken back from components/modals/, and the setAutoRotate(false) dispatch the spec named as
the change that fails quietly (losing it leaves autoplay running forever).

Note

Phase context: docs/refactor/s-phases.md.

issues.display_title: Issue #153: S6 the RoomStaging / VirtualStaging2D convergence
issues.main_description_html:
Problem

S6 (the RoomStaging / VirtualStaging2D convergence, PR #147, 72d320d) merged into development
without its manual pass. 46 files / 6.5k lines converged — 18 of 23 file pairs were byte-identical
before the phase, so the diff is large and the behaviour surface is narrow.

Two rows in the plan are the ones no static gate covers, and neither has been run:

  • §4.1 — wrong-kind rejection, both directions. The only place a collapsed acceptsImage
    predicate surfaces. The two slices differed in one substantive line, one negation apart.
  • §4.5 — byte/dimension parity, both variants. The only place a swapped geometry constant
    surfaces.

Both produce plausible-looking wrong output rather than an error. Typecheck, lint and tests all pass
either way.

What to do

Run docs/refactor/s6-staging-pair-test-plan.md. §4.1 and §4.5 are mandatory and must run for
both RoomStaging and VirtualStaging2D — one is not evidence for the other.

§4.5 is a parity check: compare output bytes and dimensions against a pre-S6 build, per
docs/refactor/standards.md. "Looks right" is not a pass.

Expected

Every scenario passes, or fails into its own issue. Sign-off section filled in at the bottom of the
plan.

Note

Hands-off subfeatures (Stitching, Image to Video, Scale Up Image) are out of scope — S6 did not touch
them and its shared ProgressList was deliberately not applied to them. Phase context:
docs/refactor/s-phases.md.
